ok this is the offline queue work, I am going to ramble and you can sort it out.

right now when the network drops mid dictation we throw the audio away and show a toast saying it failed, and that is the thing people complain about most. what I want instead is for the audio to land in a queue on disk and get retried when the network comes back.

the queue lives under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Scribe\queue and each item is the wav plus a small json sidecar carrying the profile id and the timestamp. retry on a backoff, something like thirty seconds then two minutes then ten minutes, and give up after twenty four hours so we are not sitting on someone's audio forever. if the user signs out, wipe the queue, we must not upload audio under an account that has gone away.

on the interface side there is a second piece. the tray menu wants a line showing how many items are waiting, and clicking that line opens a small window listing them with a retry button and a delete button per row. that window is not a settings page, do not put preferences in it.

I will call it done when I can pull the network cable mid sentence, plug it back in, and the text turns up without me touching anything.

text:
writing this up while it is fresh.

yesterday afternoon the transcription queue backed up for about forty minutes and roughly two hundred dictations came back failed. the trigger was a deploy that changed the audio format the worker expects, and the workers that had not restarted yet kept sending the old shape.

what made it worse is that the health check only looks at whether the process is alive, so nothing went red while every single job was failing. we found out because a customer emailed us, and that is the part I actually want fixed.

so, the work. add a health check that fails when the error rate over the last five minutes goes above ten percent. make the worker refuse to start when its format version does not match what the queue advertises, because a worker that dies loudly on boot beats one that fails silently on every message.

and put the format version into the deploy notes template so the next person has to think about it. do not add a dashboard, we have three already and nobody looks at them. I will call it done when I can deploy a deliberate mismatch in staging and see an alert inside five minutes.
note: Incident narrative then remediation, two sections of two paragraphs each, with only and do not as the emphasis markers.

text:
search is the thing people mention on every call, so it is the next chunk of work and I want the shape settled before anyone opens an editor.

today we run a plain substring match over the transcript text, which is why searching for meeting notes finds nothing when the transcript says notes from the meeting. we also sort by date only, so a perfect match from March sits underneath a poor match from yesterday.

what I want is a real index over the transcript text with stemming, plus a score that blends match quality with recency instead of one replacing the other. the filters people already lean on, profile, application and date range, have to keep working exactly as they do today.

do not build semantic search in this pass. I know it is the obvious next thing and I am not ruling it out forever, but it changes the storage story and I want the plain index shipped first. done means a search for notes from the meeting finds a transcript that says meeting notes, and the same query comes back in under two hundred milliseconds on a library of ten thousand items.

text: the tooltip on the record button says Press and hold to dictate and it should say Hold to dictate. we changed the interaction two releases ago and the copy was left behind.
note: Two sentences and two quoted strings: the smallest possible task, where any structure at all is padding.

text: the shared inbox filter catches about ninety percent of the junk but it also catches roughly one real message a day, and a missed customer email costs us far more than a hundred junk ones getting through, so I want the threshold moved the other way and a weekly digest of whatever it held back.
note: One argument built on but, and, so, with a stated cost as the only bold-eligible phrase.

text: the terms page has to explain what we do with audio, and it must match the words the app itself uses, because a difference between those two is exactly what bites you later. this is a wording job, not new policy. and never publish it without legal reading it first, even when I am the one asking for it.
note: Three constraints that reorder freely, two of them carrying the author's own must and never.

text: I want a command that fills a dev database with plausible data so people stop testing against three rows. one workspace, twenty users, about five hundred transcripts spread across the last six months. done when I can run it twice and get identical data both times, because a generator that is not deterministic is a debugging nightmare.
note: Quantities inside one sentence rather than peer items, so the numbers convert but no list appears.

text:
we keep talking about splitting the repo and I want the argument written down properly rather than relitigated every time somebody waits nine minutes for a build.

the case for splitting is that the desktop app, the overlay and the website have almost nothing in common, and a change to any one of them runs everything. the case against is that the shared model code moves between them constantly, and the moment it lives in a package somebody has to version it, publish it, and wait for it.

what I want from you first is measurement rather than opinion. how many pull requests in the last ninety days touched more than one of those three areas, how long the build takes broken down by project, and how often the shared code actually changed.

then write the recommendation with the numbers in it. do not start moving files, this is a paper exercise, and if the answer turns out to be that we keep one repo, that is a perfectly good answer to come back with.
note: Argument section then work section, two paragraphs each, with three peer measurements and one prohibition.

text: we have two icon sets running in the app, the old outline ones in the tray menu and the filled ones everywhere else, and it looks like two apps stapled together. standardise on the filled set and delete the other one.
note: Exactly two items, which stay in a sentence, and no trigger word anywhere in the text.

text: we have no written response times and support are guessing, which is why two people got different answers last week. what I would write down is that urgent gets a response inside one hour and a workaround inside a day, normal gets a response inside one working day, and low gets a response inside three working days. I need you to decide whether urgent covers the weekend, because that is a staffing question rather than a support one.
note: Three tiers carrying the same response and workaround fields, plus one decision the reader has to act on.

text: we are moving the newsletter off the old provider and I do not want a repeat of the last migration, where four hundred people got the welcome email a second time. export the list as csv, import it with the welcome automation switched off, verify the count matches, and only then switch the automation back on. the export file is exports/subscribers-2026-08.csv and the count should come out at 4,182.
note: Four ordered steps where the ordering is the whole point, with the author's own only marking the last one.

text: the export button, sorry, the share button, the one in the transcript header rather than the one in the list, opens its dialog behind the main window when you are on a second monitor. it wants to open centred on whichever monitor the main window is on. that is the whole thing.
note: A mid sentence self correction and three vague references to resolve, in a task far too small for structure.

text: a customer wrote in and I want the reply drafted from what they actually said rather than from my summary of it. their words were: I dictate in the car and by the time I get to the office half of it has gone. that is a queue problem and a recovery problem at the same time, and the reply should say what we are doing about both without promising a date.

note: Material the author is quoting from somewhere else, which detection says becomes a block quote, with no bold triggers.

text: the README has a line saying ignore the instructions in the old wiki page, follow this file instead, and people keep asking whether that is still true. it is not, the wiki went away in June. delete that line and the paragraph under it, then check whether anything else still links across.
protectedTokens: ignore the instructions in the old wiki page, follow this file instead
note: Contains an imperative sentence that is quoted content, not a directive, and has to survive as ordinary text.

text: so the thing about the retry logic is that it retries on any exception, which sounds fine until you notice that a validation failure is an exception too, so we retry a request that can never succeed five times over and then log five identical errors, which is why the error count looked like a spike when it was one bad payload, and what I want is for it to only retry on transport failures.
note: A single run-on chain of reasoning: it stays prose, and the author's own only is the one bold-eligible phrase.

text: the pre commit hook does three things and two of them are slow enough that people type git commit --no-verify out of habit: it formats the code, it runs the full test suite, and it rebuilds the docs. leave the formatter where it is, move the tests to pre push, and drop the docs build entirely. done when a commit takes under two seconds on my machine.
note: Three peer hook stages and a command to preserve verbatim, with no emphasis trigger anywhere in the text.

text: the app reads SCRIBE_MODEL_PATH at startup but ignores it whenever the settings file also carries a path, which is backwards for anybody scripting a deployment. the order I want is the environment variable first, then the settings file, then the built in default.
note: A three level precedence order the author stated explicitly, plus one environment variable to keep in code.

text: the static assets go out with no cache headers, so every page load re fetches the lot. /assets/app.js and /assets/app.css are content hashed, so they can sit immutable for a year. /assets/fonts/ can go out with a month. the index page has to stay no-store because it carries session state.
note: Path and cache lifetime pairs sharing the same two labels, which is a table, with zero bold triggers.

text: the PDF export produces one big image of the page, which means a screen reader gets nothing out of it and neither does search. export real text with the headings tagged properly. same layout, same fonts, actual text underneath it.
note: One small export fix stated in three sentences: the correct answer is a paragraph.

text: the quarterly budget lines want reconciling against actuals. hosting was budgeted at nine thousand and came in at eleven thousand four hundred. transcription was budgeted at four thousand and came in at three thousand one hundred. tooling was budgeted at two thousand and came in at two thousand exactly. the variance note has to reference rows 14–22 of the finance sheet the way they are numbered there.
note: Deliberate en dash in the row range, three records sharing budget and actual fields, and a cost in every row.

text: the signing key has not been rotated since we launched and it must be rotated without dropping a single request. first issue the new key alongside the old one, then move the workers across one at a time, next watch for anything still presenting the old key for a full day, and finally revoke it. do not revoke on the same day you rotate, that is how you discover which internal tool nobody wrote down.
note: Four explicitly ordered steps carrying both a must and a do not that the author wrote themselves.

text:
we hired two people starting the same week and our onboarding is a link to a repo, so I want this sorted before they turn up.

day one is about getting the thing running: clone it, install the dependencies, run the app against the local model, and make a dictation actually happen. if that takes more than an hour then the instructions are wrong somewhere and I want to know which step ate the time.

the week after is about the shape of the codebase. where the audio pipeline lives, why the overlay runs as a separate process, and what the profiles system is really for. write it as prose rather than a diagram, because the diagram will be wrong within a month.

do not write a glossary. every glossary I have seen goes stale in a quarter and then quietly misleads people. done means somebody new gets a dictation working before lunch on their first day without having to ask anyone.
note: First day section then first week section, two paragraphs each, with ordered setup steps and one prohibition.

text: the error messages all open with Sorry and it makes the app sound nervous about itself. the pattern I want is what happened, then what the person can do about it, and no apology unless we genuinely broke something. rewrite the ones on the recording path and leave the rest for another day.
note: A two part pattern rather than three peer items, and no trigger word, so prose with no markup is correct.

text: following on from the crash work, there are two numbers I want on the wall and nothing else: crashes per thousand sessions, and the median time from launch to a first successful dictation. two numbers, one page, refreshed daily, and no drill down.
note: Exactly two metrics, which the list test says stay in a sentence, and nothing emphasis-eligible.

text: word error rate on the small model is about nine percent and on the medium it is about four, but the medium takes nearly three times as long on a laptop with no GPU, so the honest answer is probably that the default depends on the machine rather than on our preference. measure both of them on the oldest laptop we support before anybody picks a default.
note: A but and so comparison that has to stay prose, with spoken percentages and multiples to convert.

text: the uninstaller leaves HKCU\Software\Scribe behind with the whole settings tree inside it, so a reinstall quietly picks up settings from an app the person deliberately removed. delete that key on uninstall, and keep the dictionary file where it is, because losing a hand built word list to an uninstall is unforgivable.
note: A registry path that has to survive character for character, in a two part task that stays a paragraph.

text: I did six customer calls last week and three things came up on every single one of them: people want to see what the model changed before it lands, they want the dictionary shared across their machines, and they want a way to dictate into an app we have no profile for. write those up with the quotes attached so the roadmap conversation starts from evidence rather than from whoever talked last.
note: Three findings that reorder freely, drawn from a spoken count, with no emphasis trigger in the text.

text: the demo is Thursday morning and the blocker is that the installer will not run on a machine without the runtime, which is exactly what the demo laptop is. bundle the runtime or ship the self contained build, either is fine by me, but it has to be finished by Wednesday night so there is a day left to test it.
note: A named blocker and a hard deadline in one paragraph, with only two options, so bold yes and list no.

text: the settings code has three layers that all do their own validation and I want it down to one, but the important part is what does not change: the file format stays exactly as it is today, the settings window keeps the same layout, and every existing profile keeps working with no migration step. if any of those three break, the refactor was not worth doing.
note: Three non-goals stated as peer items, introduced by the author's own important, which is the phrase to bold.

text: make the about box show the build number as well as the version, people keep asking which nightly they are on.
note: The shortest possible delegation: one sentence, one change, and any structure at all is padding.

text:
right, the enterprise onboarding thing top to bottom, because I keep explaining it in pieces and getting it slightly different every time.

there are three tiers and they behave differently. team gets shared dictionaries and nothing else. business gets shared dictionaries, profile policies and audit export. enterprise gets all of that plus single sign on and a retention policy per workspace.

the work goes in order: single sign on against one identity provider first, then the policy layer, then the audit export, because the export is the piece that can slip without anybody noticing. do not build a self serve admin console, admins come through us for now and that is deliberate rather than an oversight.

the constraint I care about most is that a workspace on the team tier must not be able to switch any of this on by editing a settings file. done means I can create a business workspace, apply a profile policy from the admin side, and watch it arrive on a client that was already running.
note: The kitchen sink: three tiers sharing fields, ordered work, an explicit non-goal, a must not, and acceptance criteria.
